analysis.one_liner: Lets workers take sexual harassment claims to court instead of forced private arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House committee without ever getting a vote, despite bipartisan sponsorship that included 3 Republican cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Many employers require workers to sign contracts before any dispute arises, agreeing to settle sexual harassment claims in private arbitration instead of court — one worker at a time, before an arbitrator the employer helps select, with no appeal. This bill would make those clauses unenforceable for sex discrimination disputes, restoring workers' right to a judge, a jury, and a public record. It was introduced with bipartisan support but never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who signed mandatory arbitration clauses and later experienced sexual harassment. They would regain the right to file in court, have a judge or jury hear the case, appeal an adverse ruling, and have the proceedings become part of the public record. Employees who face the same harasser would also be able to join together in a single case, something arbitration clauses typically bar.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employees with harassment claims blocked from court

how_it_helps.text: Voids any predispute arbitration agreement that requires arbitration of a sex discrimination dispute, meaning an agreement signed before a dispute arises cannot force a sexual harassment claim into private arbitration.
Puts the decision about whether the ban applies in the hands of a court rather than an arbitrator, preventing the employer-selected arbitrator from ruling on the scope of the clause itself.
Applies to any dispute arising on or after the date of enactment, so new harassment claims would go to court.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would face harassment claims in open court before juries, with appeal rights for workers and the possibility of group cases — increasing their legal exposure and settlement costs. Arbitration providers and employer-side defense practices would lose a stream of business.

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only sex discrimination disputes; workers facing arbitration clauses over race, age, or disability discrimination would remain subject to them, creating uneven rules for comparable claims.

Supporters of arbitration argue it can resolve disputes faster and at lower cost than court, and some workers might individually prefer it; the bill removes that option for sex discrimination claims rather than regulating how arbitration is conducted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is substantial: forced arbitration of harassment claims is widely criticized for keeping allegations secret, isolating each worker alone, and offering no appeal, all in a forum shaped by the employer. The cost falls on employers in the form of jury trials and greater litigation risk — the very exposure arbitration clauses were designed to avoid. The bill is narrowly drawn (sex discrimination only, disputes after enactment only), which limits both its help and its disruption.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, and sat there without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Cheri Bustos introduced the bill on December 6, 2017, joined as original cosponsors by Reps. Walter Jones (R), Pramila Jayapal (D), and Elise Stefanik (R).
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced.
On January 22, 2018, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law.
The bill's 5 cosponsors split 3 Republican and 2 Democratic.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place; the bill died in committee when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use mandatory arbitration clauses kept the ability to route sexual harassment claims into private, individual arbitration, avoiding public jury trials and multi-worker cases. Arbitration providers kept their business.

for.name: Rep. Cheri Bustos
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to void forced arbitration clauses for sexual harassment claims.

for.name: Reps. Walter Jones, Pramila Jayapal, and Elise Stefanik
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors the day the bill was introduced.

for.name: 2 additional Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing it to 5 cosponsors, 3 of them Republican.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership (Chair Bob Goodlatte)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the record shows only referrals to the committee and a subcommittee, no further action in two years.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was bipartisan from day one — its original cosponsors included two Republicans alongside Democrats, and 3 of its 5 total cosponsors were Republican — yet it never got a committee hearing or vote.

industries.note: These employers would lose their ability to keep harassment disputes out of court, out of juries, and out of public view. Their interest in the status quo runs directly against workers' access to court.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and employer-side defense practices
industries.note: Private arbitration of employment disputes is a business; the bill removes sex discrimination disputes from that market. Their revenue depends on the practice the bill restricts.
